prompt: Six months after a release, an auditor asks whether the dependency check ran on it. In a DevSecOps team, what makes that question answerable?

choices.text: The security engineer's sign-off on the release ticket
choices.why: A sign-off records that somebody looked at something; it does not say which checks ran on that commit.

choices.text: The pipeline run of that commit, stage by stage
choices.why: Right: the run lists every agreed check as passed or excepted, with a log per stage.

choices.text: The scanner vendor's dashboard showing zero open criticals today
choices.why: Today's dashboard describes today, not what was checked on the release half a year ago.

choices.text: The absence of any incident since the release went out
choices.why: No incident says nothing about whether anybody looked; that is the gap the written list closes.

prompt: A colleague set `advice.ignoredHook` to false on their machine. They push to the course's CI server and see `To ~/ci/linkbox.git` and the branch moving, and nothing else. What should they conclude?

choices.text: The pipeline passed quietly, because a clean run prints nothing
choices.why: A clean run prints a line per stage and `pipeline passed`; silence is not a pass.

choices.text: No pipeline ran: the hook is missing or not executable, and the commit is unchecked
choices.why: Right: with the hint switched off, a hook that is missing or not executable leaves no sign but the missing `remote:` lines, and the commit is unchecked.

choices.text: The server rejected the push, and the branch did not move
choices.why: The branch did move; a rejected push says so in its own message.

choices.text: The run started in the background, and its result will arrive later by e-mail to whoever pushed
choices.why: This server runs the pipeline inside the hook and prints as it goes; there is no background run or mail.

prompt: The secret check flags `password = "changeme"` in a test fixture that creates a throwaway user in a temporary database. Of the three ways out of triage, which one fits?

choices.text: Fix it, by moving the value into the vault and rotating it
choices.why: There is nothing to protect: the value opens a database that exists for one test.

choices.text: Except it until a date, with a reason and a named owner
choices.why: An exception is for a real finding that cannot be fixed yet; this one is not real.

choices.text: Not real: tune the check so it stops reporting it
choices.why: Right: a finding that is not real is answered by tuning, so the check stops saying it.

choices.text: Leave it open, since it does no harm
choices.why: A finding in no state is exactly how a pipeline teaches a team to ignore it.

prompt: The rule lesson 7 argues and the rest of the course leans on: a check breaks the build only for something the person who broke it can ___.
By lesson 19, how many entries does linkbox's `ci/stages` list have?
A team adds a full dynamic scan to every push and the pipeline goes from five minutes to twenty. Following lesson 2's budgets, what should happen to the scan?

choices.text: Mark the stage allowed to fail, so pushes are not blocked by it
choices.why: That is the end of the road lesson 1 named: a check nobody reads.

choices.text: Keep it on every push, since a finding is a hundred times cheaper early
choices.why: The hundredfold figure has no study behind it, and twenty minutes makes people batch their changes.

choices.text: Move it to the nightly list on main, with failures sent to a person
choices.why: Right: it still runs every day on what is actually on main, and nobody's push waits for it.

choices.text: Drop it, because a check that cannot run early is not shifting left
choices.why: A slow check goes further right to a place that can afford it; it is not dropped.

prompt: Boehm and Basili's 2001 list put late defects at up to a hundred times the cost on large systems. For small, non-critical systems, what ratio did the same item give? Answer the first number of "N to 1".
A colleague's release script reads hosts from `targets.txt` with `while read -r h; do …; done <targets.txt` and ends with `echo deployed`. What change from lesson 2 does it need?

choices.text: `set -x`, so every command it runs is printed
choices.why: Tracing shows what ran; with no file nothing runs, and the script still ends in success.

choices.text: A guard that fails when the file is missing
choices.why: Right: a test before the loop that exits non-zero; a missing input makes the loop run zero times and the script carry on to its last line, exit 0.

choices.text: Quoting `$h` everywhere it is used inside the loop body
choices.why: Good practice, and unrelated to a list that is not there.

choices.text: Running it under cron, so it starts from a clean environment
choices.why: Cron changes the environment, not what happens when the file is missing.

prompt: The nightly crontab line runs the pipeline, and on its first night the test stage fails with `uv: command not found`. The same line works from your shell. What is the cause?

choices.text: The cached image layers were cleared by the rebuild the night before
choices.why: The rebuild is the second list and runs after the tests; the failure is in finding a program.

choices.text: uv refuses to run when no terminal is attached to standard output
choices.why: uv runs fine without a terminal; the server's hook runs it the same way.

choices.text: Cron's minimal PATH leaves out `~/.local/bin`, where uv lives
choices.why: Right: that is why the lesson's crontab sets PATH on its first line.

choices.text: A leftover `.venv` from the laptop made the stage refuse
choices.why: The nightly run clones into a fresh directory, so there is no leftover environment.

prompt: Match each check to the place on the line where lesson 2's budgets put it.

pairs.left: A scan of the staged lines for secrets
A rebuild of the image with no cache
A new advisory against what is running
Static analysis of the service's code

prompt: A service passes Bandit and the project's Semgrep rules with no finding. Which of these defects could still be in it? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A response with no Content-Security-Policy header
choices.why: Right: a header is a property of the HTTP answer, which only exists when the program runs.

choices.text: A published advisory against the version of Flask it pins
choices.why: Right: that flaw is in code the project did not write, which is the dependency audit's job.

choices.text: A route that should not exist at all, written correctly
choices.why: Right: correct code doing the wrong thing is a design question, and no rule has its shape.

choices.text: An f-string query reaching `execute()` in a scanned file
choices.why: That is exactly the shape both B608 and the project's own rule match, so a clean run rules it out in the files scanned.

prompt: Tired of B101 in the tests, a teammate adds `skips: [B101]` to `bandit.yaml`. What does that cost?

choices.text: Nothing, since an assert is harmless wherever it is
choices.why: Under `-O` Python drops every assert, so one guarding a decision in the service stops checking anything.

choices.text: The tests stop running, because pytest relies on the check
choices.why: pytest relies on assert itself, not on Bandit; skipping a check changes what Bandit reports and nothing else.

choices.text: A false negative in the service's own asserts
choices.why: Right: an `assert` guarding a decision in the service goes unreported; scoping the skip to the tests keeps the check where it matters.

choices.text: Bandit refuses the file, because a skip needs a path
choices.why: A global skip is valid configuration; that is what makes it tempting.

prompt: A team adds a new static analyser as a stage. Its log lists twelve findings and the pipeline prints `passed`. What is the first thing to check?

choices.text: Whether the tool exits non-zero when it reports a finding
choices.why: Right: that is Semgrep's `--error` trap; a tool that reports and exits 0 makes a stage that passes whatever it found.

choices.text: Whether the twelve findings are false positives
choices.why: Worth knowing later, and it does not explain a stage passing with findings in its log.

choices.text: Whether the stage is listed before or after the tests in `ci/stages`
choices.why: Order decides what runs first, not whether a finding fails the stage.

choices.text: Whether the tool's rules came from a registry
choices.why: Where the rules come from changes what is found, not what the exit status says about it.

prompt: Match each situation to the word lesson 3 uses for it.

pairs.left: A rule flags `shell=True` with a command built from a request parameter
B105 flags `PASSWORD_LABEL = "Password"` in a form
A new route that writes and checks no token, with no rule about it
No finding on a query written with `?` and a tuple of values

prompt: A query's column name has to be inserted from a fixed tuple, and B608 flags it. Which suppression does lesson 3 accept?

choices.text: A bare `# nosec` at the end of the line
choices.why: A bare one switches off every check on that line, including ones written next year, and says nothing a reviewer can check.

choices.text: `# nosec B608: the name comes from the COLUMNS tuple` on that same line
choices.why: Bandit reads every word after nosec as a check id: the reason becomes a warning per word.

choices.text: A comment above giving the reason, and `# nosec B608` on the line
choices.why: Right: the check is named, the reason is there for a reviewer, and the summary still counts it.

choices.text: `skips: [B608]` in `bandit.yaml`, with a comment
choices.why: That removes the check from the search too, where the injection was a true positive.

prompt: Rule 10031 is a false positive on linkbox's search today, and a teammate wants to set it to IGNORE so the log is clean. Why does lesson 4 keep it at WARN?

choices.text: Because IGNORE makes ZAP exit with status 3
choices.why: Status 3 is a scan that could not finish; IGNORE only drops a rule's matches from the output.

choices.text: Because the file works per rule, not per page
choices.why: Right: IGNORE would also hide a real case on a page written later, one that turns escaping off.

choices.text: Because a false positive breaks the build until it is fixed
choices.why: A WARN does not break the build; only a FAIL does.

choices.text: Because the escaping is not under any test yet
choices.why: It is: lesson 3's test with an apostrophe already holds the escaping.

prompt: A service's admin pages sit behind a sign-in. The nightly baseline scan, run with no credentials, reports no finding. What does that result say?

choices.text: That the admin pages send the right headers too
choices.why: The scanner never reached them; it says nothing about pages behind the sign-in.

choices.text: That the service has no injection flaws anywhere
choices.why: The baseline is passive and sends nothing built to provoke a failure, so it would not find one.

choices.text: That the anonymous pages passed the passive rules
choices.why: Right: until the scanner signs in, a clean result describes the anonymous surface only.

choices.text: That the scanner was blocked, since a real scan always finds something
choices.why: A scan with no finding is a valid result; linkbox's own scan passed with one WARN and sixty passes.

prompt: A baseline scan run without `-I` ends with `FAIL-NEW: 0 … WARN-NEW: 3 … PASS: 58`. What exit status does `zap-baseline.py` return?
To save time, a developer proposes running the dynamic scan against `flask run` on their laptop instead of the image the pipeline built. What is wrong with that?

choices.text: Flask's development server refuses connections from containers
choices.why: It accepts them if bound to the right address; the problem is what is being scanned.

choices.text: It scans a server that is not the one deployed
choices.why: Right: its headers and error pages are not the ones deployed; the scan has to read the image that ships, started the way the Dockerfile starts it.

choices.text: ZAP's passive rules need a database with real data
choices.why: A per-run staging deliberately holds nothing real, and the rules work on it.

choices.text: The scan would take longer than on the image
choices.why: Speed is not the objection; the findings would describe something nobody deploys.

prompt: A manager asks for ZAP's full scan against production on Sunday night, "when nobody is using it". What answer does lesson 4 support?

choices.text: Yes, provided `-silent` is passed so ZAP makes no outside calls
choices.why: `-silent` stops ZAP's own update checks; it does nothing about the requests the scan sends to the target.

choices.text: Yes, because at low traffic it cannot affect users
choices.why: It writes into real data, sends real e-mails and orders, and can page on-call whatever the hour.

choices.text: Only against the anonymous pages, which hold no data
choices.why: An active scan submits every form it reaches, anonymous ones included.

choices.text: No: only at a staging built for the run
choices.why: Right: an active scan writes and breaks things, so it points at a staging holding nothing real, and never at production.

prompt: pip-audit prints 40 rows for three packages, and the monthly report asks how many flaws the service carries. What does lesson 5 say to count?

choices.text: The rows, since each one is a separate advisory to fix
choices.why: Most flaws arrive twice, as a GHSA record and a PYSEC record, so rows count the database, not the problems.

choices.text: The distinct CVE ids among the aliases
choices.why: Right: the CVE says which flaw, and it is the id every other tool and team will recognise.

choices.text: The packages, since one upgrade fixes everything in a package
choices.why: Three packages is the size of the work, not the number of flaws in the service.

choices.text: The distinct fixed versions in the last column
choices.why: Several flaws share a fixed version, and one flaw can list two.

prompt: Match each fact about a finding to the source it comes from.

pairs.left: `AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N` and a score of 8.2
A probability of 0.03 for the next thirty days
Listed since March, with reliable evidence of exploitation
Whether this service ever runs the vulnerable code
pairs.right: Your own reading of the advisory

prompt: There is more to fix than time. Put the findings in the order of attention lesson 5 suggests, first at the top.
items: A CVE on CISA's KEV list, whatever its score
A reachable flaw with a high EPSS probability
A reachable flaw with a high CVSS score and a low EPSS
An unreachable flaw, left for the next routine update

prompt: A project pins only `django==4.2.0` in its requirements file. Trivy reports two findings and pip-audit eleven. What explains the gap?

choices.text: Trivy's database is older than PyPI's
choices.why: Databases do drift by a day or so; that does not turn two into eleven on one file.

choices.text: pip-audit counts each flaw twice, so the real number is five or six
choices.why: Doubling is real, and it still leaves more than Trivy found; the lists themselves differ.

choices.text: Trivy skips Django because it is a web framework
choices.why: Trivy read Django from the file; it reads every line of a file it recognises.

choices.text: pip-audit resolves what Django pulls in; Trivy reads one line
choices.why: Right: one tool audits the transitive packages Django pulls in today, the other the line the file holds; a file pinning only direct packages makes them disagree.

prompt: One internal package cannot be resolved from PyPI, and the `sca` stage keeps failing. A teammate proposes dropping `--strict`. What does that change?

choices.text: The package is skipped, and "not checked" reads as "clean"
choices.why: Right: the package is skipped with a warning and the stage passes having never looked at it.

choices.text: Advisories with no fixed version stop breaking the build, and only warn
choices.why: `--strict` is about collecting packages, not about which advisories fail the audit.

choices.text: pip-audit stops resolving transitive packages
choices.why: It still resolves everything it can; only the failure to collect is forgiven.

choices.text: The audit switches from PyPI to osv.dev
choices.why: The source is chosen with `-s`; `--strict` has nothing to do with it.

prompt: A cloud access key was pushed to the team's repository this morning. Put the response in lesson 6's order, first at the top.
items: Revoke the key at the provider
Issue a new key, delivered somewhere that is not the repository
Remove the key from the code
Read the provider's logs for its use between the commit and the revocation
Decide whether the history is worth rewriting

prompt: A database password was committed three months ago and deleted the next day. The team lead proposes `git filter-repo` and a forced push as the fix. What does lesson 6 say is missing?

choices.text: A second scan with `gitleaks dir`, to confirm the files are clean
choices.why: The files have been clean since the day after; the danger is the value, which still works.

choices.text: Changing the password, which every copy still holds
choices.why: Right: every clone, fork and backup made in three months still holds it; a rewrite changes one copy, and only revoking the value makes the others harmless.

choices.text: A `.gitleaksignore` entry, so the pipeline stops reporting it
choices.why: That records a dead finding; this one is not dead until the password is changed.

choices.text: Nothing, as long as everybody clones again after the push
choices.why: Re-cloning helps the people who do it; forks, backups and the contractor's laptop are untouched.

prompt: In which of these cases does lesson 6's argument make rewriting the history worth its price?

choices.text: An API token that was revoked and replaced at the provider yesterday
choices.why: Once revoked it opens nothing; a rewrite would cost every clone to silence a scanner.

choices.text: A test value that opens a temporary database
choices.why: That is not a secret at all: what makes a value a secret is what it opens.

choices.text: A spreadsheet of customers' addresses committed by mistake
choices.why: Right: personal data cannot be revoked, so removing it from the copies is part of limiting the damage.

choices.text: A webhook URL whose signing secret was rotated earlier this week
choices.why: Rotated means dead; the old value in the history verifies nothing now.

prompt: A rotated token keeps failing the `secrets` stage. Instead of adding its fingerprint to `.gitleaksignore`, a teammate proposes disabling the `generic-api-key` rule. What is the difference?

choices.text: None in practice: both leave the same finding out of the report
choices.why: For this finding, yes; for the next secret the rule would have caught, the difference is everything.

choices.text: A fingerprint expires on its own after ninety days
choices.why: A line in `.gitleaksignore` stays until somebody removes it; nothing expires.

choices.text: Disabling the rule makes gitleaks exit 0 even on a specific provider's token
choices.why: Specific rules such as GitHub's would still fire; the loss is the generic catch-all.

choices.text: One finding is excused; without the rule, every later secret passes
choices.why: Right: the fingerprint names one finding, so a new secret tomorrow is still reported; disabling the rule lets every one of them through.

prompt: A team relies on a gitleaks pre-commit hook. Which of these secrets can reach the server without the hook ever reading them? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: One committed with `git commit --no-verify`
choices.why: Right: that flag skips the hook.

choices.text: One committed by a new colleague on a fresh clone
choices.why: Right: hooks live in `.git/hooks`, which a clone does not copy.

choices.text: One that arrives in a branch merged from somebody without the hook
choices.why: Right: the hook reads only what is staged in this commit on this laptop.

choices.text: One staged and committed normally on a laptop where the hook is installed
choices.why: That is the one case the hook does read, and it refuses the commit.

prompt: A token is added in a repository's first commit and the file stays unchanged through nine more commits. How many findings does `gitleaks git` report for it?
A colleague proposes that a stage warn by exiting 2, "since it sits between a pass and a failure". What goes wrong?

choices.text: Nothing: the number is arbitrary as long as the runner knows it
choices.why: The runner reads the number and nothing else, so it has to be one no failure produces by accident.

choices.text: Bash reserves 2 for syntax errors, so the stage would not run
choices.why: A stage exiting 2 runs fine; the trouble is what else exits 2.

choices.text: A mistyped option also exits 2, and would pass
choices.why: Right: Python exits 2 on an unknown option, so a run that checked nothing would go on as a warning.

choices.text: ZAP would stop translating its warnings
choices.why: ZAP's own 2 is translated by the `case`; the clash is with every other program.

prompt: A scanner that crashed or timed out has said nothing, so its stage breaks the build. Lesson 7 calls this failing ___.

A branch adds a helper that writes a report to a fixed path under `/tmp`. Bandit raises a medium finding; the author says nothing calls the helper yet and asks for a warning. What does lesson 7 decide?

choices.text: Warn, because unreachable code exposes nothing
choices.why: "Nothing calls it" is a claim no check holds; it is false the day somebody wires it up.

choices.text: Pass, with an exception dated a month ahead
choices.why: An exception is for a fix that cannot land yet; this one can land in the same change.

choices.text: Break: the author fixes it in this change
choices.why: Right: it is fixable now by the person who pushed it, by deleting it, using `tempfile`, or suppressing it with a reason.

choices.text: Add it to a baseline, since it is new code
choices.why: A baseline records what existed when the scanner arrived; new code is what the gate answers for.

prompt: A team switches on Semgrep for a five-year-old service and gets three hundred findings in old code. Which plan does lesson 7 support?

choices.text: Break on all three hundred until they are fixed
choices.why: That stops the team on day one, and the gate is switched off by day three.

choices.text: A baseline so only new findings break, with an owner and a budget to shrink the number
choices.why: Right: whoever pushes answers for what they added, and the old number has somebody bringing it down.

choices.text: Three hundred exceptions dated a year ahead
choices.why: Exceptions are for single findings with short dates; a year-long batch is a baseline by another name.

choices.text: Warn on all of them, so nothing blocks a push
choices.why: Three hundred old warnings bury the next real finding.

prompt: Today is 2026-10-28. The only advisory in the audit has a fixed version and an exception in `ci/exceptions.txt` holding until 2026-11-02. What exit status does `ci/gate.py` return?
A Dockerfile installs a monitoring agent with `curl -o /usr/local/bin/agent …` in a `RUN` line. Trivy's report on the image lists nothing for it. What does that tell you about the agent?

choices.text: That its version has no published advisory
choices.why: Trivy never learnt its version; there was nothing to look up.

choices.text: Nothing: no package record names it, so the scan never saw it
choices.why: Right: an image scanner reads package records, and a clean report is a statement about the lists, not about the image.

choices.text: That it was scanned as a binary and found clean
choices.why: Trivy does not recognise code from its bytes; a C binary records nothing it can read.

choices.text: That the download failed and the file never made it into the image
choices.why: The file can be there and working; it is only invisible to the scan.

prompt: In the distroless image, one CVE against the source package `krb5` is reported once per binary package Debian builds from it. How many rows does that one CVE produce?
The image stage only counts findings that no rebuild can fix. Which of these events turn one of them back into work? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Its status changes from `affected` to `fixed`
choices.why: Right: a rebuild on the refreshed base now installs the fix, and the build has to happen.

choices.text: The CVE appears on CISA's KEV list
choices.why: Right: exploitation in the wild is a reason to change base or patch, whatever the gate says.

choices.text: The base image's release reaches its end of life
choices.why: Right: `affected` on a supported release means a fix may come; past end of life nothing comes.

choices.text: The same CVE is reported against a second binary package
choices.why: That is one flaw counted twice, the krb5 case; it adds rows, not work.

prompt: A team on `python:3.13-slim` sees the image gate fail on four HIGH findings with fixed versions, in urllib3, msgpack and setuptools. None of them is in their requirements. What is the lasting fix?

choices.text: Add the three packages to requirements.txt at their fixed versions
choices.why: The findings are in pip's own vendored copies, which the project's pins do not touch.

choices.text: Upgrade pip in the image on every build
choices.why: It clears today's four, and the next pip will vendor the next urllib3 and its next advisory.

choices.text: Two stages, with pip left behind in the first
choices.why: Right: the final image carries the installed packages and not pip, which is needed to install and is dead weight afterwards.

choices.text: Drop `--ignore-unfixed` so the gate judges every finding
choices.why: That would break on the Debian findings nobody can fix, which is the opposite of what is needed.

prompt: A colleague rewrites the image stage as `trivy image … "$image" | grep -q CRITICAL && exit 1; exit 0`. What happens on the day the build tags the image under a different name?

choices.text: The stage breaks, because Trivy exits 1 when the image is missing
choices.why: Trivy does exit 1, but the pipe hands grep its output and the script ignores Trivy's status.

choices.text: Trivy pulls the image from Docker Hub instead
choices.why: There is no linkbox on Docker Hub; the lesson's capture shows the remote lookup refused.

choices.text: The push stage refuses the missing image, which catches it
choices.why: Nothing guarantees that; the check the stage existed for has already passed nothing.

choices.text: Trivy cannot run, nothing is found, and every image passes from then on
choices.why: Right: reading output instead of the exit status turns "did not run" into a pass.

prompt: An image declares `USER 65532`, and a hurried manifest starts it with the user set to 0. Which of these controls still hold? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A read-only root filesystem
choices.why: Right: it refuses the write whoever asks; root got `Read-only file system` on `app.py`.

choices.text: Dropping every capability
choices.why: Right: with an empty bounding set, root cannot chown, bind a low port or open a raw socket.

choices.text: `no-new-privileges`
choices.why: Right: it holds whatever the process is; no executed file can raise its privilege.

choices.text: The `USER` line in the image
choices.why: That is the one control the override removes: it is the user a container starts as when nothing says otherwise.

prompt: Lesson 9's thread program runs in a container started with `--pids-limit 50`. How many threads does it report starting before one is refused?
A container runs with a read-only root and `/tmp` mounted `tmpfs` with `noexec`. Somebody who can make the application write a file to `/tmp` writes `tool.py` there. Can it run?

choices.text: No: `noexec` stops anything in `/tmp` from running
choices.why: It stops the kernel executing the file as a program; it says nothing about an interpreter reading it.

choices.text: No: a read-only root stops the write in the first place
choices.why: `/tmp` is a writable mount of its own; the root being read-only does not cover it.

choices.text: Yes: `python3 /tmp/tool.py` reads it as input
choices.why: Right: the interpreter is the program and the file only its input, so `noexec` does not apply; the filesystem controls take away the easy ways, not every way.

choices.text: Yes, but only as root
choices.why: The user does not matter here; user 65532 runs the interpreter just as well.

prompt: A distroless image has no setuid file anywhere under `/usr`. Why does lesson 9 still set `no-new-privileges`?

choices.text: Because Docker refuses `--cap-drop ALL` without it
choices.why: The two flags are independent; each was tested on its own.

choices.text: Because it turns on the seccomp filter
choices.why: Seccomp is on by default; `NoNewPrivs` is a separate line in the status.

choices.text: Because it stops the process from writing setuid files
choices.why: It does not stop a write; it stops an executed file from running with more privilege.

choices.text: It protects the next image, not this one
choices.why: Right: a later base or a tool copied in brings a setuid file nobody reviews, and the flag costs nothing to a program that never needed new privileges.

prompt: A service fails in its container with `Operation not permitted` on one system call the default seccomp profile refuses. A teammate proposes `--security-opt seccomp=unconfined`. What does lesson 9 recommend instead?

choices.text: A custom profile that allows that call and nothing else
choices.why: Right: unconfined removes the whole filter for one call; a custom profile keeps every other refusal.

choices.text: Running the container with `--user 0` so the call is allowed
choices.why: The filter refused the call to root with default capabilities too; the user is not what it checks.

choices.text: Adding `--cap-add SYS_ADMIN` and keeping the default profile
choices.why: That hands the container one of the broadest capabilities to get one call through.

choices.text: Unconfined in staging only, and the default profile in production
choices.why: Staging earns its name by matching production; a difference here hides the failure until deployment.

prompt: A deploy job runs `kubectl apply -f k8s/` into a namespace enforcing the restricted profile. It prints a PodSecurity warning, then `deployment.apps/api created`, and the job goes green. What should the job have done?

choices.text: Nothing more: `created` means the API server accepted the pods
choices.why: Pod Security Admission judges pods, and a Deployment is not one; its pods are refused later, out of sight.

choices.text: Run `kubectl apply` a second time, to clear the warning
choices.why: The warning is a forecast that the pods will be refused; applying again changes nothing.

choices.text: Wait with `kubectl rollout status` and fail when the rollout does not finish
choices.why: Right: the ReplicaSet's refusal lives only in the events, so the job has to check that pods actually came up.

choices.text: Switch the namespace to `warn` so the pods are admitted
choices.why: That weakens the rule to make the job pass; the pods should state what the profile asks.

prompt: Match each refusal or fill-in to the object that produces it in lesson 10's namespace.

pairs.left: A Deployment with no memory limit, refused at `kubectl create`
A bare pod with no limit, given 128Mi
A fifth replica refused when four fill the namespace
A pod that does not state `runAsNonRoot: true`

prompt: Under lesson 10's policy, a developer pushes an image built on their laptop to the registry as `localhost:5000/linkbox:hotfix` and deploys it. What happens?

choices.text: Refused, because the tag is not `main`
choices.why: The rule checks the start of the name, not the tag.

choices.text: Accepted: the rule reads a name only
choices.why: Right: a name is not proof the pipeline built the image; anything pushed to that registry passes, and lesson 14's signatures close the gap.

choices.text: Refused, because the image was not scanned
choices.why: Admission reads the manifest; it has no way to know whether a scan ran.

choices.text: Accepted with a warning naming the unscanned image
choices.why: The binding's action is Deny or nothing; no warning about scans exists.

prompt: After an expression error blocked a deploy, a teammate sets the admission policy's `failurePolicy` to `Ignore`. What has the team given up?

choices.text: Nothing while the expressions are correct
choices.why: The setting decides the cases where they are not, and that is exactly when it matters.

choices.text: The warnings Pod Security Admission prints at apply time
choices.why: Those come from a different mechanism and are unaffected.

choices.text: The ability to bind the same policy to more than one namespace at once
choices.why: Binding is the binding's job; `failurePolicy` is about evaluation errors.

choices.text: The guarantee itself, on every object the rule fails to judge
choices.why: Right: an object the rule fails to judge gets in, which is lesson 7's scanner that did not run, so the policy fails closed with `Fail`.

prompt: A namespace's ResourceQuota allows 10 pods and 1024Mi of `limits.memory`. Each pod of a Deployment declares a 192Mi limit. It is scaled to 8 replicas. How many pods run?
A team's image ends with `USER appuser`, a name rather than a number, and the pod sets `runAsNonRoot: true`. What does the kubelet do?

choices.text: Starts it, because the name is not `root`
choices.why: The kubelet does not trust a name; `appuser` could be uid 0 in that image's files.

choices.text: Refuses it: a name does not say whether the user is root
choices.why: Right: the kubelet needs the numeric user the image declares, such as lesson 8's 65532, to know it is not 0.

choices.text: Starts it as user 65532 instead
choices.why: The kubelet does not pick a user; `runAsUser` would, and the pod does not set it.

choices.text: Admission refuses the Deployment before the kubelet sees it
choices.why: Neither admission rule of the lesson reads the image's user; the kubelet checks it at start.

prompt: Match each question to the kind of scan lesson 11 would answer it with.

pairs.left: Is anything listening on the office network that nobody put on a list?
Are the sales team's laptops, rarely on the office network, patched?
Was any image shipped last quarter built with this morning's CVE?
Which Deployments run images that never went through the pipeline?

prompt: An unauthenticated scan flags a Debian server for an OpenSSH advisory, from the version in its banner. Debian fixed it by backporting the patch without changing the upstream number. Which scan settles the question?

choices.text: A second unauthenticated scan from another network
choices.why: It reads the same banner and infers the same wrong version.

choices.text: A credentialed scan
choices.why: Right: it reads the host's package database, exact version and backport included, instead of inferring from a banner.

choices.text: `trivy image` on the server's base image
choices.why: The server is a host, not an image; its packages live in its own database.

choices.text: An active DAST scan of the SSH port
choices.why: A web scanner tests HTTP applications; it says nothing about which OpenSSH package is installed.

prompt: `trivy config` reports DS-0002, "no USER", on a Dockerfile whose final base image already runs as user 1001. Which answer does lesson 11 prefer?

choices.text: Turn DS-0002 off for the whole repository
choices.why: That loses the check for the Dockerfile that really runs as root.

choices.text: Change the base to one that sets no user, then add a `USER` line
choices.why: Changing a good base to satisfy a rule is backwards; the image is already right.

choices.text: Ignore it, since the image is what runs
choices.why: An unrecorded silence is a finding nobody can tell from one nobody read.

choices.text: Write `USER` in the final stage, so the file says what is true
choices.why: Right: the image does not change, and a later base that runs as root still gets a non-root container.

prompt: In a meeting, a client says it is fine for your team to run a network scan of their offices next week. What does lesson 11 say is still missing?

choices.text: Nothing, provided the scan is unauthenticated
choices.why: An unauthenticated scan is still traffic that looks like the first step of an attack.

choices.text: A licence for Nessus Professional
choices.why: The tool is the smaller question; the permission comes first.

choices.text: A signed scope in writing
choices.why: Right: it names the addresses, the window, the kind of scan and a person who stops it; a sentence in a meeting is not authorisation.

choices.text: An agent installed on each of their machines first
choices.why: Agents are one way to read hosts; they do not replace the authorisation.

prompt: A team gates every push on `trivy fs .`, which reports zero, and drops the image scan as redundant. What does lesson 11 say they lost?

choices.text: Nothing, since `fs` and `image` share one engine and one database
choices.why: One engine, yes, reading different files: the base image's packages are not in the repository.

choices.text: The base image's Debian packages
choices.why: Right: they exist only once the base is pulled; the zero of `fs` is about the pins, and the image's 162 come from Debian's database inside it.

choices.text: The misconfiguration checks on the Dockerfile
choices.why: Those come from `trivy config`, a separate mode either way.

choices.text: The secrets in the Git history
choices.why: That is gitleaks' stage, which they kept.

prompt: Match each situation to the control lesson 12 says would have caught it.

pairs.left: A CI step pipes a vendor's install script from `curl` into `bash`, and the vendor's storage was altered
pairs.right: Compare the script's SHA-256 with the published one before running it

pairs.left: A workflow uses a third-party action at `@v3`, and the tag is moved to new code
pairs.right: Refer to the action by its full commit hash

pairs.left: An internal package's name is free on PyPI, and installers add the company index with `--extra-index-url`
pairs.right: Point installers at one index the company controls

pairs.left: A popular package's publishing account is taken over and a release appears an hour ago
pairs.right: A cooling-off period before adopting new releases

right_distractors: A higher CVSS threshold in the gate

prompt: A team writes its lock with a hash for every file on the same afternoon a stolen account published a malicious release, and the lock picked that release. What does the hash do for them?

choices.text: Refuses the release, since its content differs from the real one
choices.why: There is no other file to differ from: the hash was taken from the malicious file itself.

choices.text: Nothing: it pins the malicious file
choices.why: Right: a hash judges later files, not the first one; the defence for the first is not adopting a release until it has aged a few days.

choices.text: Flags it, because pip compares hashes with the index's records
choices.why: pip compares with the requirements file; it trusted what the team wrote down.

choices.text: Says who built the file, which exposes the stolen account
choices.why: A hash says which bytes, not who made them; that is a signature's and provenance's job.

prompt: A vendor's update carried a backdoor and was signed with the vendor's own certificate, because signing ran after a compromised build. What does that show?

choices.text: That the certificate had been stolen
choices.why: It had not; the build was altered and the real certificate signed its output.

choices.text: That signing has no value and can be dropped
choices.why: A signature still says who published; it simply does not say what went into the build.

choices.text: That a signature vouches for a publisher only
choices.why: Right: it says who published, not that the artefact matches its source; provenance and an isolated build answer that.

choices.text: That reviewing the source code would have found it
choices.why: The repository never contained the backdoor; the source the victims could review was fine.

prompt: Of these defences, which one does lesson 12 say removes dependency confusion as a class?

choices.text: Registering each internal name on PyPI as a placeholder
choices.why: It closes the door for the names claimed and no others.

choices.text: A cooling-off period on new releases
choices.why: That answers stolen accounts; a confused name can be old enough to pass it.

choices.text: Reading every new name in the lockfile's diff
choices.why: That is the defence against typosquatting, and it relies on a careful reader.

choices.text: Installers pointed with `--index-url` at a single index the company controls
choices.why: Right: one index decides in one place which name comes from where.

prompt: pip installs a file only if its SHA-256 is one the requirements file lists when it runs with the option ___ given on the command line.
A team keeps syft's SBOM of every image and plans to rescan them each month with a different vendor's scanner, without the images. What does lesson 13 say to do before relying on that?

choices.text: Convert every SBOM to SPDX, since it is the ISO standard
choices.why: The SPDX file did worse with Trivy: it was not even read as Debian.

choices.text: Nothing: an SBOM is a standard, so any reader gets the same answer
choices.why: syft's list scanned by Trivy gave zero Debian findings where the image gave 162.

choices.text: Delete the images, since the SBOM now replaces them
choices.why: Keeping the digest and the image is what lets a doubtful result be checked directly.

choices.text: Test that writer and reader pair on an image whose findings are already known
choices.why: Right: a zero from the pair where the image has findings is a result to see in a test, not in an incident.

prompt: Why does linkbox's `sbom` stage read the image by the tag of the run's commit rather than by `main`?

choices.text: Because syft cannot read a tag that has been pushed twice
choices.why: syft reads any tag; the problem is what the tag will point at later.

choices.text: Because `main` moves and the commit's tag does not
choices.why: Right: an SBOM naming `main` would describe a different image after the next push; the commit's tag is never moved by the pipeline.

choices.text: Because `main` is only pushed on the nightly run
choices.why: `push` moves `main` on every run on the main branch.

choices.text: Because the registry refuses to serve `main` to syft
choices.why: The registry serves both tags; nothing refuses.

prompt: A syft run writes a CycloneDX SBOM with 3000 components: 2900 of type `file`, 99 of type `library` and 1 `operating-system`. How many entries does the SPDX file from the same run count in `packages`?
To save time, a team generates its SBOM with `syft dir:.` on the repository instead of on the image. What does lesson 13 say that list gets wrong?

choices.text: Nothing, if the requirements pin every package
choices.why: Even fully pinned, the repository holds no base image and does hold the test tools.

choices.text: It is the same list in a different order
choices.why: It finds pins twice, pytest and its packages, and no Debian package at all.

choices.text: It misses the Python packages, which syft reads only from images
choices.why: syft found every Python pin in the repository, twice over.

choices.text: It describes the source tree, not what ships
choices.why: Right: test tools that never ship appear and the base image's packages do not; an SBOM describes the thing it was made from.

prompt: A licence review of an SBOM finds one Python package whose licence field is empty. What does lesson 13 say that blank means?

choices.text: The package is in the public domain
choices.why: Nothing recorded is not a licence of any kind.

choices.text: The package has the same licence as the image it ships in
choices.why: An image has no single licence; it carried 84 distinct names.

choices.text: A question somebody has to answer by reading the package
choices.why: Right: the generator recorded nothing, which is not the same as there being nothing to record.

choices.text: The SBOM is corrupt and has to be generated again from the image
choices.why: The rest of the document read correctly; one field the tool could not fill is not corruption.

prompt: A deploy script runs `cosign verify … registry/app:main` and, when it passes, `kubectl set image deploy/app app=registry/app:main`. What is wrong with it?

choices.text: cosign cannot verify a tag, only a digest
choices.why: It can: it resolves the tag to its digest at that moment, as the lesson's refusals showed.

choices.text: Both name a tag; deploy the digest that was verified
choices.why: Right: a tag moves between the two steps; a verification answers for the digest it checked, so that exact reference is what gets deployed.

choices.text: `kubectl set image` ignores tags and always pulls the newest image
choices.why: It uses the reference it is given; that is exactly why the reference should be a digest.

choices.text: The verification should run after the pull, not before
choices.why: Order matters, and the fix is naming the same bytes in both steps, not swapping them.

prompt: Match each situation to what `cosign verify --key ci.pub` reports for it.

pairs.left: The tag was moved to an image nobody signed
An image signed with a colleague's own key
The commit's tag, still on the digest the CI signed

right_distractors: A list of the image's vulnerabilities

prompt: To make verification easy, a team publishes `cosign.pub` in the same registry repository as the images, and deploy scripts fetch it from there. What does lesson 14 say is wrong?

choices.text: Public keys must be kept secret, like the private key
choices.why: A public key is useless for signing; the question is who can replace it.

choices.text: A registry cannot store a file that is not an image
choices.why: The registry already holds signatures and attestations beside the image; storage is not the issue.

choices.text: Whoever pushes images there also pushes the key
choices.why: Right: their own signatures then verify; the key has to come from somewhere the verifier trusts, such as a protected repository or the admission controller.

choices.text: cosign refuses a key fetched over HTTP
choices.why: The lesson's registry is plain HTTP on localhost; the problem is trust, not transport.

prompt: linkbox's pipeline writes provenance for every image and signs it with a key on the same laptop where the code is written. Which SLSA Build level does it honestly meet? Answer the number.
A manager proposes skipping the image scan at deploy time for any image the CI signed, "since signed means checked". What does lesson 14 answer?

choices.text: Agreed: the signature proves the image has no known vulnerability
choices.why: It proves who vouched; tomorrow's advisories were not in yesterday's scan.

choices.text: A signature names who vouched, not that it is safe
choices.why: Right: the CI signs whatever passed its stages, so a gap in the scan is signed too, and looks more trustworthy for it.

choices.text: Agreed, provided the signature is keyless
choices.why: Keyless changes whom you trust for the identity, not what the signature claims.

choices.text: Signed images are already rescanned by cosign at verification
choices.why: `cosign verify` checks a signature against a key; it reads no advisories.

prompt: A developer raises one range in `requirements.in` and runs `uv pip compile … -o requirements.txt` over the existing lock. Only that package moves; the rest keep their old versions. Why?

choices.text: The other packages have no newer releases
choices.why: They may well have; the compiler kept them because they still satisfy the ranges.

choices.text: `--exclude-newer` froze every package except the one whose range changed
choices.why: The date limits what can be chosen; it does not pick which packages move.

choices.text: The compiler keeps the pins that still fit
choices.why: Right: every pin already in the output that still fits is kept, so the lock changes as little as possible and a review reads only what moved.

choices.text: Hashes stop the other packages from changing version
choices.why: Hashes pin the bytes of a chosen version; they do not stop a compile choosing another.

prompt: A lock is compiled with `--exclude-newer` a week behind today. Yesterday a package in it published the fixed version for an advisory the gate now reports. What does lesson 15 say happens, and what is the answer?

choices.text: The compile picks up the fix anyway, because security releases bypass the date
choices.why: The date has no such exception; it looks only at what was uploaded before it.

choices.text: The fix is held back too; a person makes an exception for that one package
choices.why: Right: the cost of a cooling-off period is real, and the answer is a decision with an owner, not moving the rule.

choices.text: Remove `--exclude-newer` for good, since it blocks fixes
choices.why: That also removes the protection against a release published from a stolen account this morning.

choices.text: The compile fails until the date is moved past the fix
choices.why: It does not fail; it resolves to the newest version before the date, and the gate keeps reporting.

prompt: A service uses a signing library only to sign tokens that the same service checks later. The library has an advisory against signing with no planned fix. What does lesson 15 point to?

choices.text: Keep it pinned with an exception, since verification is unaffected
choices.why: That row is for a service that only verifies others' signatures; this one signs.

choices.text: Fork the library and patch the side channel locally
choices.why: That makes the team the maintainer of cryptographic code, the most expensive answer there is.

choices.text: Update to the newest release, which is bound to contain a fix
choices.why: The project has said in writing that no fix is planned; there is nothing to update to.

choices.text: `hmac` from the standard library
choices.why: Right: nobody else verifies the token, so it needs a message authentication code, not a signature, and no dependency at all.

prompt: Put the steps of linkbox's offline build, from lesson 15, in the order they run.
items: A virtual environment with pip is made in `.build`
`pip download --require-hashes` fetches the wheels the lock names
pip installs from `/wheels` with `--no-index`, checking each hash again
The installed packages are copied into the distroless stage

prompt: A team says it pins every dependency "so that we never have to update". What does lesson 15 say pinning is for?

choices.text: To make each update a decision somebody takes, with the pipeline's checks run on it
choices.why: Right: and the further a pin falls behind, the larger the jump when an advisory forces it.

choices.text: To stop advisories from being reported against old versions
choices.why: Advisories are published whatever a project pins; the gate reports them all the same.

choices.text: To replace a dependency without changing code
choices.why: Replacing touches every call site; pinning changes no code.

choices.text: To make the build faster by skipping resolution
choices.why: Speed is a side effect at most; the point is what enters production and when.

prompt: A public project wants its tests to run on pull requests from forks. Its workflow uses `pull_request_target` and checks out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha`, "so the tests get the secrets". What should it use instead?

choices.text: `pull_request_target` with `persist-credentials: false` on the checkout
choices.why: That keeps the token out of `.git/config`; the stranger's code still runs with the base repository's privileges.

choices.text: `pull_request_target` with every action pinned by commit
choices.why: Pinning protects against moved tags; it does not change whose code runs with the secrets.

choices.text: The `pull_request` trigger
choices.why: Right: it runs a fork's code with a read-only token and no secrets, which is all testing somebody else's change needs.

choices.text: `pull_request_target` with `permissions: contents: read`
choices.why: The secrets are still available to the job, and the code it runs is still the fork's.

prompt: A workflow step reads `run: ./deploy-preview.sh "${{ github.head_ref }}"`, where the branch name comes from the pull request's author. How does lesson 16 make it safe?

choices.text: The quotes around the expression already make it safe
choices.why: The platform expands `${{ … }}` before the shell sees the script; quotes are part of the text it is pasted into.

choices.text: Move the expression into an `env:` entry and have the script read `"$BRANCH"`
choices.why: Right: through an environment variable the value reaches the shell as data, never as code.

choices.text: Pin `deploy-preview.sh` to a commit hash
choices.why: The script is the repository's own; the problem is the text pasted into the line that calls it.

choices.text: Run the step only on `push` to main
choices.why: That hides the step from pull requests rather than fixing it, and the preview was the point.

prompt: A team's shared build server adds the `jenkins` user to the `docker` group, so jobs can build images without `sudo`. What has every job been given?

choices.text: The right to build images, and nothing beyond it
choices.why: The socket accepts any request the daemon accepts, including a container that mounts the host's filesystem.

choices.text: Read access to the other users' home directories
choices.why: It is far more than reading; the daemon runs as root.

choices.text: The same privileges as whichever user installed Docker on that server
choices.why: The daemon runs as root whoever installed it.

choices.text: Root-level privileges on the host, through a daemon that runs as root
choices.why: Right: Docker's own documentation says the group grants root-level privileges to the user.

prompt: Which of these can change what a CI job runs, and so belong to the pipeline's attack surface? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The author of a third-party action named by tag
choices.why: Right: a tag can be moved to new code, as tj-actions showed.

choices.text: A stranger who opens a pull request
choices.why: Right: their code is what the job checks out.

choices.text: Whoever controls the machine the runner is on
choices.why: Right: the runner is part of the trust.

choices.text: A user who only reads the published release notes
choices.why: Reading what was published influences nothing the job runs.

prompt: A company keeps one persistent self-hosted runner, warm caches included, for both its pull-request tests and its release job that signs images. What does lesson 16 say is wrong?

choices.text: Nothing, provided the pull-request workflow uses the read-only token
choices.why: The token protects the repository, not the machine the code runs on or what it leaves there.

choices.text: Test jobs leave things the release job runs on
choices.why: Right: a modified tool or a poisoned cache from a test job is under the release job next; separate runner groups, or a fresh machine per job, prevent it.

choices.text: Warm caches make the signed images differ from the tested ones
choices.why: That is a reproducibility worry, not the one the lesson names.

choices.text: Self-hosted runners cannot sign images
choices.why: They can; the question is what else has run on the machine that does.

prompt: An AWS role trusts GitHub's token service with `aud` = `sts.amazonaws.com` and a `StringLike` condition `sub` = `repo:acme/*`. Whose workflows can assume it?

choices.text: Only the main branch of acme's deployment repository
choices.why: Nothing in the pattern names a repository or a branch.

choices.text: Every repository on GitHub, since the issuer signs for all of them
choices.why: The `sub` condition still limits it to the owner acme; the broader mistake is a role with no `sub` at all.

choices.text: Any job in any acme repository, present or future
choices.why: Right: a wildcard where an exact value belongs trusts every branch, pull request and future repository under the owner.

choices.text: Only jobs that name an environment
choices.why: An environment changes the shape of `sub`; the wildcard matches that shape too.

prompt: A deploy role's condition names `repo:acme/billing:ref:refs/heads/main`. The team renames the repository, and the old name is later registered by somebody outside the company. What does lesson 17 say a safer condition uses?

choices.text: The `jti` claim, which is unique per token
choices.why: `jti` changes on every token; a role cannot be bound to it.

choices.text: The repository's numeric ids
choices.why: Right: `repository_id` and `repository_owner_id` stay the same through a rename; a condition on a name is met by whoever owns the name later.

choices.text: A wildcard on the branch, so the rename does not break deploys
choices.why: That widens the role and does nothing about who owns the name.

choices.text: The `iat` claim, so only recent tokens are accepted
choices.why: Every token is recent when it is used; the time says nothing about whose repository asked.

prompt: A Vault role gives CI tokens `token_ttl=5m`, and a long job renews its token every four minutes. What else does lesson 17 say the role should set?

choices.text: A `token_max_ttl` close to the length of a run
choices.why: Right: the TTL is how long it lives unless renewed; the maximum is the ceiling renewals never pass, so the token does not outlive the job.

choices.text: A shorter `token_ttl`, such as thirty seconds
choices.why: A job renewing more often still renews forever without a ceiling.

choices.text: A `list` capability, so the job can find its secrets
choices.why: Listing widens what the token can see and has nothing to do with how long it lives.

choices.text: Nothing: renewal is how a token stays valid for exactly one job
choices.why: Nothing ties renewal to the job; a leaked token renewed by somebody else lives on too.

prompt: `ci/sign.sh` now reads the signing password through `ci/vault-read.sh linkbox-main …`, and the file in `~/ci/keys` is gone. A branch called `debug` changes `sign.sh` to print the password. What does its run print?

choices.text: The password, since the branch's script runs on the CI server
choices.why: The script runs, and it has nothing to print: the role refuses the branch's login.

choices.text: Nothing, because the CI server masks secrets in logs
choices.why: Masking is a courtesy, not a control, and this CI does none; the refusal comes from Vault.

choices.text: A Vault token, which the attacker can use for five minutes
choices.why: No Vault token is issued; the login is refused before one exists.

choices.text: Vault's refusal: the `ref` claim does not match the role, so there is no password to print
choices.why: Right: the identity token says `refs/heads/debug`, the role is bound to main, and the script fails closed.

prompt: To avoid storing the signing password, a team gives the CI server a long-lived Vault token whose only power is to create five-minute tokens for each run. What has it achieved, by lesson 17's argument?

choices.text: A pipeline with no long-lived credential
choices.why: The token-creating token is long-lived, and it unlocks everything the run tokens can reach.

choices.text: The secret moved one step: the long-lived token is now the secret zero
choices.why: Right: a short-lived credential is only as good as the way it is obtained; signed identity removes the need for one.

choices.text: Federated identity, as hosted services do it
choices.why: Federation presents a statement signed by the CI, not a token handed out by a stored token.

choices.text: Nothing different from dev mode's root token
choices.why: It is narrower than root; the point is that it is still a stored, long-lived secret.

prompt: A team turns on auto-merge for base image digest updates, "since the image scan and the signature run on every one". What does lesson 18's table say they have not covered?

choices.text: The signature, which a bot cannot produce
choices.why: The pipeline signs whatever passes its stages, bot's change or not.

choices.text: How the new system packages behave
choices.why: Right: no stage exercises the new system libraries, and auto-merge is for what a green pipeline judges completely.

choices.text: The advisories, which the image scan does not read
choices.why: Reading advisories against the image is exactly what the image scan does.

choices.text: The digest, which Dependabot cannot update
choices.why: The documentation says Dependabot updates a digest pin to the new digest.

prompt: Put the steps of remediating one dependency in the order lesson 18's table gives them, from the first to the last.
items: The bot finds that a newer version exists
A scanner says an advisory applies to the pinned version
The bot writes the change, and the pipeline checks it is written correctly
The tests show, as far as they reach, that the new version still behaves
A person, or a rule a person wrote, lets the change in

prompt: A tool moves a package's version in a hash-pinned lock and leaves the old version's hashes beside it. The team's test stage installs with plain `pip install -r`, without `--require-hashes`. What happens?

choices.text: The install refuses the package, because the hashes do not match
choices.why: Without the mode on, as here, nothing compares the hashes with the file that arrives.

choices.text: The security gate breaks, since the hashes are stale
choices.why: The composition gate reads versions and advisories, not hashes.

choices.text: Every stage passes, and the team ships a lock whose hashes protect nothing
choices.why: Right: the change looks right and is not, and only a pipeline that checks hashes would notice.

choices.text: pip recomputes and rewrites the hashes during the install
choices.why: An installer reads the requirements file; it does not edit it.

prompt: A team wants its bot's patch updates of test-only packages to merge on their own. Which conditions does lesson 18 say must hold first? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The branch is protected, so the merge waits for every required check
choices.why: Right: auto-merge is the pipeline acting as reviewer, so all of it has to run.

choices.text: A check that did not run counts as failed
choices.why: Right: lesson 7's fail-closed rule, applied to merging.

choices.text: The bot's token cannot push to `main` directly
choices.why: Right: a bot that can push to main needs no auto-merge to bypass the pipeline.

choices.text: The cooldown is switched off for those packages, so merges are not delayed
choices.why: The table allows these merges after the cooldown, not instead of it.

prompt: In `renovate.json`, the setting that holds a release back until it has been public for a number of days, Renovate's name for a cooldown, is ___.
A team's Rego rule checks only `input.spec.template.spec.securityContext.runAsNonRoot == true`, the pod level. Which Deployment does it wrongly pass?

choices.text: One whose pod sets nothing and whose container sets `runAsNonRoot: true`
choices.why: That one runs as non-root; the pod-only rule would wrongly refuse it, not pass it.

choices.text: One whose pod says `true` and whose container says `runAsNonRoot: false`
choices.why: Right: a container's own setting overrides the pod's, which is why lesson 19 writes the helper twice.

choices.text: One with an image named by digest
choices.why: How the image is named has nothing to do with the user it runs as.

choices.text: One with two containers that both set nothing
choices.why: The pod-level check sees the pod's `true` and passes it, which is correct: both inherit it.

prompt: A policy package holds 6 `deny` rules, and conftest runs it against a directory of manifests containing 4 YAML documents. How many tests does conftest report?
A rule reads `deny contains msg if { input.spec.replicas > 3; msg := "too many replicas" }`. conftest evaluates it on a Service, which has no `spec.replicas`. What happens?

choices.text: The rule raises an error and conftest exits 2
choices.why: Rego does not raise on a missing field; the expression is simply undefined.

choices.text: The missing field is read as 0, and the rule passes
choices.why: Nothing is read as 0; the line has no value at all.

choices.text: Nothing: the rule adds no message
choices.why: Right: the line cannot be evaluated, which counts as not true, so the body does not hold and the Service passes this rule.

choices.text: The rule fires, since a missing replica count is unsafe
choices.why: Rego concludes only from lines that hold; it has no notion of a missing value being unsafe.

prompt: A Dockerfile has `USER 1000` in its build stage and no `USER` in its final stage. What does lesson 19's `policy/docker.rego` report?

choices.text: Nothing: a numeric non-root user is declared
choices.why: It is declared in a stage that does not ship; only the final stage decides who the container runs as.

choices.text: That the final stage sets no USER
choices.why: Right: the helper reads only the last stage's USER instructions, and there are none.

choices.text: That USER 1000 is not 65532
choices.why: The rule accepts any number but 0; 65532 is only the example in its message.

choices.text: That the build stage must not set a USER
choices.why: No rule says that; a USER there is merely irrelevant to the image that ships.

prompt: A conftest policy reads files. Which of these can such a policy decide? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Whether a manifest names its image by a moving tag
choices.why: Right: the image reference is written in the file.

choices.text: Whether a container declares a memory limit
choices.why: Right: the limit is a field in the manifest.

choices.text: Whether the image that runs was signed by the CI
choices.why: That needs the registry's answer, which a check over files cannot fetch.

choices.text: Whether a pinned dependency has an advisory today
choices.why: That needs an advisory database, which is the composition stage's job.

prompt: A team fixed seven high findings this quarter, in 2, 3, 3, 5, 6, 8 and 90 days. What is the median time to remediate, in days, the figure lesson 20 says to report beside the 90th percentile?

One quarter the `181+` column of a team's debt report empties, while the number of findings fixed stays where it was. The tracker dates each finding from its latest opening. What should be checked first?

choices.text: Whether the team fixed its oldest findings in a push
choices.why: The fixed count did not move, so the old findings did not leave by being fixed.

choices.text: Whether old findings were closed and reopened
choices.why: Right: reopening resets the age to zero; the count of findings reopened, reported beside the debt, shows it.

choices.text: Whether the SLA for low findings was raised
choices.why: An SLA changes the past-SLA column, not the age of a finding.

choices.text: Whether the bucket edges were moved
choices.why: Fixed edges are worth keeping, and nothing here says they changed; the dates did.

prompt: Over two quarters, the share of high findings fixed within SLA rises from 78% to 95%, while the number of high findings falls and the number of medium ones rises by about the same. What does lesson 20 point to?

choices.text: Findings moved from high to medium severity
choices.why: Right: a high reclassified as medium gets 90 days instead of 30, and the SLA is met with no change to the code.

choices.text: A faster team, since the high SLA is being met
choices.why: The shift between the two rows is the tell; speed would not move findings from one severity to another.

choices.text: A new scanner that finds more medium findings
choices.why: A new scanner would add findings, not take them away from the high row.

choices.text: A data set too small for percentages
choices.why: Size is worth checking, and it does not explain the two rows moving in step.
